properties.description:
Discuss the intended Query composer experience and query-language capabilities before starting implementation. Continue from the parent task and the existing conversation; distinguish agreed requirements from open questions and assistant proposals. Preserve the discussion verbatim as it proceeds so implementation can resume without context loss.

Topics already raised: complex and nested expressions; multiline authoring; typed function signatures, argument help and diagnostics; explicit editable initial queries; draft versus applied expressions; a shared component across views; and agent/MCP access to the same query construction and contextual completion capabilities. The previous popup-versus-panel recommendation is an unaccepted proposal, not a requirement.

Current access observation: query_read exposes ordinary discover/complete/evaluate operations, while graph-specific completions and the selected frontend composer context are not exposed through that operation. Discuss the intended agent experience and boundaries; do not treat a proposed implementation as already accepted.

User request starting this discussion (verbatim):
Time has come to do graph://planning-26535745-4644-4770-af7c-1980c773377b/entries/5fd282b0-e831-4b6c-8d0b-3e9b254d291c.json

Lets start by you adding as children task of the query rework a task for a discussion.

Discussion — TypeScript direction

User (verbatim):
Perfect

now my vision is the following for the filter / query system.

The way i see it and the more it develop the more i think its moving toward a kind of script. Now i am not big on us developing our own scripting language. I think it would be a waste of time. I am very attached however to the ergonomy of being able to compose the query through the autocomplete alone.

My though are lingering around autocompleting typescript script however i expect this choice would open tons of questions i am unaware of thats one of the reason i want to discuss it.

Assistant (verbatim; proposal and question, not an accepted decision):
I think **TypeScript is a strong candidate**. It gives us existing parsing, type checking and contextual completion machinery. We would still design the query API and its authoring experience. [TypeScript language-service documentation](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Language-Service-API).

Your autocomplete requirement goes further than ordinary code completion: choosing an operation should insert its syntax, guide you through its arguments, offer relevant components or engine instances, and then suggest valid continuations. The resulting text could remain ordinary TypeScript. We would need to demonstrate that this works from an empty query through to a complete one.

There is one immediate consequence for our earlier design. Suppose these functions return query objects:

```ts
materialized(frontend) && hasComponent(Task)
```

In TypeScript, `&&` would apply its normal truthiness behavior; it would not combine those objects into a filtered query. [TypeScript’s explanation of truthiness](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html#truthiness-narrowing).

An illustrative API could express that as:

```ts
materialized(frontend).where(hasComponent(Task))
```

Autocomplete could construct that whole expression, including the parentheses and arguments. Boolean predicates could still use ordinary `&&` and `||`.

**Would you be comfortable with function/method composition like this replacing `&&` / `||` between query operations, provided the entire expression remains constructible through autocomplete?** The names above are only illustrative; this would establish how closely we want to follow TypeScript’s existing semantics.

Discussion — compilation, debugging and instance references

User (verbatim):
> Would you be comfortable with function/method composition like this replacing `&&` / `||` between query operations, provided the entire expression remains constructible through autocomplete?  



Yep



What about the compilation, are we able to compile expression(s) on the frontend ? Are we able to debug them with break point, ... ?



What aboue when the time come to reference instance for the autocomplete, for example when you want to filter a node with a task created by a specific user ?

Assistant (verbatim):
Yes. **Compilation can happen entirely in the browser.** TypeScript provides compiler APIs that turn source text into JavaScript, and its Playground demonstrates browser-based TypeScript tooling. We could check the draft while editing, then compile and execute on Apply. Full type checking is a separate step from merely stripping the types. [Compiler API](https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Compiler-API), [Playground tooling](https://www.typescriptlang.org/dev/sandbox/).

**Breakpoints are feasible through browser developer tools.** By giving each script an identifiable source and generating source maps, we can debug its original TypeScript: pause, step through execution and inspect variables. [Source-map debugging](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/javascript/source-maps).

Putting those debugger controls directly inside our composer would require additional integration; an editor with autocomplete does not supply that automatically. Also, a frontend breakpoint would not automatically pause work delegated to another engine. If a script constructs a query for later execution, debugging its construction and inspecting its execution are separate concerns.

**For instance autocomplete, we would combine TypeScript information with graph lookup.** TypeScript can tell us what kind of reference an argument expects; the relational engine supplies the actual candidates.

For your example, an illustrative expression could be:

```ts
materialized(frontend)
  .where(hasComponent(Task))
  .where(references(CreatedBy, nodeRef("graph://…")));
```

The names are illustrative. At the reference argument, the proposed experience would be:

1. The declared relation/API metadata tells us which kinds of nodes are appropriate.
2. Autocomplete lets you search for a user by name, showing enough context to distinguish matching names.
3. Selecting a user inserts their stable node reference, so renaming them does not change whom the query targets.
4. Candidate lookup stays bounded and follows an explicit scope through the local engine.

That means searching actual instances is an additional completion capability we must supply. It can share the same candidate provider between the UI and MCP, while TypeScript handles the code-level completions.

**For the first version, would debugging through the browser’s developer tools be acceptable, or do you want breakpoints and stepping directly inside the composer?**

Agreement from this exchange: the user accepts function/method composition in place of boolean operators between query operations, provided the whole expression remains constructible through autocomplete. The debugger placement and instance-completion design above remain proposals pending discussion.

Discussion — user experience and shared application API

User (verbatim):
> For the first version, would debugging through the browser’s developer tools be acceptable, or do you want breakpoints and stepping directly inside the composer?



I am not even decided yet if i want to go typescript.



I think I might designing the solution before defining the needs because i am unsure of the exact boundary and shape of it.



Let leave aside typescript for now and talk a bit about the user experience.



I would say that the first thing for me is while i have some use case where i have a hard time to see how we could express that in a one line input field. A one line input field would make sense aswell for the filter ui component in other cases so we can't fully discard the current design.



Here are the two use case i have in mind that illustrate that :



Single line : While i am using activity board, i don't want to have to compose a full script just to filter the task created by me. I want to click filter, select the appropriate operator in a click and select myself and it just work.



Multi line : Through the graph editor i am trying to understand what we currently have in term of component type / data type / node / ... How our data / our components are structured so i can guide you to reshape them. To do that i need to be able to compose advanced request. I probably don't want to do that in one line and i might want to enable / disable some part. I basically need "full access" to be able to investigate. I need to be able to adjust at the very list the color of the rendered node for each group of node i include in the query.





The challenge is that the later need quite the advanced setup but the first one need to keep it dumb simple so its enjoyable for the simple use cases.



Ideally i would like to keep it unified so user can grow into the feature aswell and don't need to lear two system.

User follow-up (verbatim):
Third use case that come to mind is using the same API for the frontend ui aswell that why the typescript come to mind.

Assistant (verbatim; synthesis and open question):
That third use case makes the shared API a central requirement. And you’re right: my debugger question moved into implementation before we had established the needs.

I now understand three uses of the same query capability:

- **Everyday filtering:** “Filter → Created by → Me.” The view supplies the existing context; you add a restriction without having to author a script.
- **Investigation:** inspect components, types and their relationships; compose more elaborate requests; enable or disable parts; distinguish groups of results through color. Autocomplete should remain useful throughout.
- **UI development:** application code constructs requests through the same API, with the same meanings and behavior as the user-facing query system.

**Unification should mean shared concepts and continuity of work.** A simple filter should be something you can expand and inspect further without translating it into another system. The compact experience should remain sufficient for everyday work, while the advanced experience gives you room and control. Your earlier requirement still applies: the view’s initial query must remain accessible and editable.

The color requirement adds another need: retaining which nodes belong to which groups, so you can distinguish and investigate those groups. How grouping and appearance are authored remains open; we don’t need to choose syntax or panel layout yet.

TypeScript helps explain the appeal of a shared API for application code. It does not yet settle the language or presentation used in the composer.

One useful boundary to explore next: **would “full access” also include a request such as “within this scope, count how many nodes use each component type, and color those types according to that count”?** That would establish whether the investigation experience needs computed analyses as well as selecting and combining existing nodes and edges.

Clarification of earlier exchange: TypeScript has not been chosen. Acceptance of the illustrative function/method composition must not be treated as acceptance of a scripting language, execution architecture or debugger design. The discussion is now focused on needs across simple filtering, advanced investigation and programmatic UI use. The computed-analysis example is an open question, not an accepted requirement.

Discussion — capabilities defined by the host environment

User (verbatim):
> One useful boundary to explore next: **would “full access” also include a request such as “within this scope, count how many nodes use each component type, and color those types according to that count”?** That would establish whether the investigation experience needs computed analyses as well as selecting and combining existing nodes and edges.  



Honestly the way i see it the environment in which the filter / query component is used determine whats available.



graph editor might decide it want to expose the ability to change color for group of node, activity board might want to do the same for task background color for example but we can agree that graph and activity board are two very different thing and trying to find a common ground for both would only restrict what the user could do insteed if each provide the right environment.

Assistant (verbatim):
Yes. I was treating the available capabilities as something we had to settle globally. **In your model, the environment defines what is available, and the shared composer provides the way to discover and compose it.**

For example:

- The Graph editor can expose node groups, traversal and node coloring.
- The Activity board can expose task filtering and task-background coloring.
- Each environment can expose further capabilities without requiring every other view to support them.

The common experience is how you discover operations, understand their arguments, select instances, compose expressions and apply them. Users learn that interaction once, then discover the capabilities relevant to their current environment.

That also means **autocomplete is how the environment explains itself**. It needs to communicate what is available here, what each operation accepts and what can follow—not just complete names the user already knows.

The ownership boundary remains important: graph rendering capabilities belong to the Graph editor; reusable data-query capabilities belong to the engine and its contributors. The composer brings those available capabilities together.

One consequence to retain for later: an expression may depend on a particular environment. If reused elsewhere, unavailable capabilities must be made clear. We should not reduce each environment’s capabilities merely to make every expression universally portable.

Requirement clarified by the user: the environment using the shared filter/query component determines the available capabilities. Graph editor and Activity board may expose their own presentation and investigation capabilities; unification must not constrain them to a lowest common set. Concrete capability inventories, language, UI layout and cross-environment reuse behavior remain to be designed.

Discussion — Composable query environments

User (verbatim):
> For example:
>
> - The Graph editor can expose node groups, traversal and node coloring.
> - The Activity board can expose task filtering and task-background coloring.
> - Each environment can expose further capabilities without requiring every other view to support them.



On the opposite side of things however the environment should be composable, i don't want each view to have to provide a full environment by themselve, for example being able to query node and filter them based on the component they have or the "archetype" they match  is probably something something recurring across views.

Assistant (verbatim):
Yes. **Each view should assemble its environment from reusable capabilities**, adding only what is specific to that view.

I would distinguish three kinds of contribution, without making them a rigid hierarchy:

- **General graph querying:** finding nodes, filtering by components or archetypes, following relations, and combining results.
- **Domain capabilities:** task properties, authors, statuses, and other concepts supplied by the relevant contributors. These can be useful in several views.
- **View capabilities:** turning results into graph groups with node colors, or applying background colors to Activity board tasks.

That also corrects my earlier example: traversal need not belong specifically to the Graph editor. The graph and board could both reuse it when useful.

The reusable contribution should carry its argument information, documentation and any instance-selection support with it. A consuming view should not have to recreate those merely to expose the operation through autocomplete. Likewise, frontend code should be able to use the underlying capability without going through the composer.

**Autocomplete would present the composed environment as one coherent whole.** Users would see the operations relevant to what they are building, without needing to understand which module supplied each one.

This preserves both requirements: common capabilities are implemented once, and individual views can extend what users can do. I’ve recorded composable environments as a requirement in the discussion task.

Requirement clarified by the user: Query environments must themselves be composable. Views should reuse shared capabilities such as querying nodes and filtering by components or archetypes, rather than each supplying a complete independent environment. The three contribution categories and packaging of discovery metadata above are an assistant proposal, not an accepted implementation design. Language and concrete composition API remain undecided.

Discussion — Disposable frontend prototype

User (verbatim):
> I would distinguish three kinds of contribution, without making them a rigid hierarchy:



In some sense you are right that we can kind of categorize the contribution to the environment but i think you are trying to establish patterns where they will appear natuarrly. The way i see it all those contribution to the environment are "API, modules, instances", ... Ok some API provide those capabilities you mention but it doesn't means that all would fit in on of those three.



To come back to the user experience though i think that what we need to focus on.



I suggest we do a mock ui component which is front end only and is not functional  (in the sense it has no real effect, but i can still use it in the app) and we fill with placeholder autocompleting hardcoded data so its easy to play around with and we can discard it once we reached the form that satisfy us.



Commit everythings on the three repositories so we can start with this mock ui component being the only thing we have in the worktree changes and we can commit it for reference / tracability and revert the commit easily afterward.



Starting design is the existing ui component in term of frontend layout and composition.

Direction confirmed: Do not establish a fixed classification of environment contributions. They may be APIs, modules, instances or other contributions, and patterns should emerge from use. Focus now on an interactive frontend-only mock using hardcoded autocomplete data, beginning from the existing component layout and composition. Apply must not affect real queries/data. Preserve current work in all three repositories before the mock so it can be isolated and discarded later. TypeScript and the eventual language/API remain undecided.

Checkpoint commits created before the prototype: TheBroccoli 927cf3e; BtrTemplate 64f486d; PersoTemplate 2468c2d.

Discussion — Define the experience endpoints before the transition

User (verbatim):
ok good but took too much time to achieve considering the request and looking at the files you had to edit it clearly shows we have architecture issues but let focus on the immediate task.

One of the challenge is the seemless and progressive transition between a **simple** single line input filter for what is shown toward more advanced function of the view and more generally the capability untill you reach full control over what exist.

This reinforce my vision of typescript in some sense because while its not typescript that run in the browser to produce the view the javascript that run was produced from typescript and typescript provide important context to understand and provide a good autocompletion experience.

The way i see we first need to define the extreme of the "range" what do we want those to be like and then think how we seemlessly move between those extremities.

Assistant (verbatim):
Yes. Defining those endpoints first gives us something concrete to evaluate language and UI choices against.

**At the simplest end**, I would describe the experience as: “I am looking at tasks; show me those created by me.” The view already supplies the context. I open Filter, choose Created by, choose Me, and apply it. Autocomplete carries the interaction; I need no knowledge of programming, engine instances or how the view obtains its data.

**At the most advanced end**, I would describe it as an editable program with access to the environment’s contributed APIs, modules and instances. I can name intermediate results, combine operations, compute values, enable or disable portions, inspect results, and use whatever presentation capabilities are available. For your graph investigation, that could mean several independently defined groups, each with its own selection and color.

The simple filter should remain understandable within that advanced experience. Expanding it should reveal the work I already composed, so learning more builds on what I know.

I understand your interest in TypeScript here as **continuity with the application’s own code and the information needed to discover its capabilities**. That is a useful criterion to retain while we define the experience.

There is one distinction I would settle about the advanced endpoint before designing the transition: **do you imagine opening and editing the program that currently defines the view itself, or writing a separate program that controls the view through its exposed capabilities?** Both can use the same APIs, but they give the user different starting points and different degrees of ownership over the view.

User direction: Define the simplest and most advanced ends of the experience before designing the seamless progressive transition. Preserve autocomplete-led simplicity and eventual access to the composed environment's full capabilities. TypeScript remains under consideration, with continuity with frontend code and contextual completion as motivations. Assistant endpoint descriptions are proposals; whether advanced editing concerns the defining view program or a separate controlling program remains an open question. No implementation change was made in this discussion round.

Discussion — Provisional advanced endpoint at the range of the view

User (verbatim):
> There is one distinction I would settle about the advanced endpoint before designing the transition: **do you imagine opening and editing the program that currently defines the view itself, or writing a separate program that controls the view through its exposed capabilities?** Both can use the same APIs, but they give the user different starting points and different degrees of ownership over the view.  



The way i see it for our immediate use case and its quite blurry for me honestly but being able to reach the range of the view itself would already be incredible.

Assistant (verbatim):
That gives us a useful provisional target: **start by filtering what the view shows, and progressively reach the ability to control the view through its available capabilities.** The exact relationship with the view’s source code can stay open for now.

For the Graph editor, the advanced experience could let you express something like:

- Include component types as one group and data types as another.
- Give each group its own color.
- Choose which relations to show and how far to explore them.
- Enable or disable either group independently.
- Adjust the layout and navigate to a particular result.

You would be able to understand and edit that whole setup, with autocomplete helping at every step.

At the simple endpoint, “Created by → Me” remains a small, direct interaction. At the advanced endpoint, you have several independently editable instructions governing the view.

I suggest using that graph investigation as our first concrete advanced example in the mock. We can establish what composing and editing it should feel like, then work out how someone grows into it from the simple filter.

Clarification: The user considers reaching the range of the view itself a valuable immediate target, while explicitly describing their vision as blurry. This does not settle whether users edit the original defining program or a separate controlling program. The graph investigation and proposed mock progression above remain assistant proposals for discussion, not an instruction to implement them yet.

Discussion — Entry point as a node in the view graph

User (verbatim):
> For the Graph editor, the advanced experience could let you express something like:



I would say it dependent the entry point honestly, there our entry point is a filter for visibility + content in the view so it make sense that the predicate signature we are completing through the ui propose an environment in that sense based on the ui component we access it from but in the end it just part of the view behavior and if we climb in the "levels" it raise the capabilities available to use.



Basically our entry point is a node of the graph of the view itself.

Assistant (verbatim):
That makes **the selected node and its signature** the starting point of the experience.

When I open the filter, I am editing a particular part of the view’s behavior. Its signature tells me what I need to produce, and its context supplies the data, APIs and instances available there. Autocomplete guides me within that situation.

Moving outward would reveal how that expression participates in the surrounding behavior. I could then select and edit a broader part of the same view graph, with the context and capabilities appropriate to that location.

That gives the range a clearer meaning:

- **Local:** change one predicate, such as “created by me,” through a small, guided interaction.
- **Broader:** navigate the surrounding view graph and work on other behavior nodes, eventually reaching the scope needed to control the view.

The continuity requirement is that **my original filter remains identifiable inside that broader context**. I can understand where it is used, return to it and keep editing it.

One consequence of your graph model: moving “up” could have several possible paths. We should show the relationship we are following rather than assume every node has one parent.

For the mock, I would explore an action that reveals **the surrounding view behavior that uses this predicate**, while keeping the predicate selected. That would let us test the experience of expanding context before choosing the language or its implementation.

User clarification: The entry point is a node of the graph of the view itself. For a visibility/content filter, the predicate signature and accessed UI component determine the relevant environment. Climbing levels reaches broader behavior and capabilities. Do not interpret this as a fixed classification of contributions or as a globally fixed simple/advanced capability list. The precise graph representation and navigation relationships remain open. Assistant suggestions about revealing context, selection retention and multiple outward paths are proposals; no mock change is authorized by this clarification alone.

Discussion — Programming scope

User (verbatim):
> That gives the range a clearer meaning:



Yeah in reality the range is the programming scope.

Assistant (verbatim):
Yes—**programming scope** captures it.

The filter opens editing at a particular point in the program, with an expected signature and the names, values and APIs available in that scope. Expanding the experience reveals more of the surrounding program and lets you choose which scope to work in.

The mock should therefore explore **editing and navigating programming scopes**, with autocomplete following the current context. A single-line filter and a larger editor become different presentations of that same experience.

Terminology clarified by the user: The range being discussed is programming scope. Concrete language, scope representation and navigation UI remain to be explored; this round makes no code changes.

Discussion — Programming scope and illustrative granularity

User (verbatim):
yep and when i talk about scope i really mean it honestly in the programming meaning. Like a function scope, an expression scope and argument in the expression basicaly down to a granular point toward the whole program. That our range.

Assistant commentary (verbatim):
I’ll record that clarification: the range runs from an individual argument or expression through its enclosing function to the whole program.

User correction (verbatim):
Exact boundary was an example not an instruction that it should be like that precisely.

Assistant commentary (verbatim):
I’ll correct the record so your examples remain illustrative and the exact boundaries stay open.

Assistant (verbatim):
Understood. Those examples illustrate **programming granularity**; they do not prescribe fixed endpoints or a particular sequence of levels.

The direction is to navigate and edit different parts of the program, with context and autocomplete following where you are working. **The exact boundaries and navigation remain open.**

Record clarification: The user’s examples explain programming granularity. They do not establish prescribed endpoints or a fixed hierarchy/navigation sequence. Concrete boundaries, navigation and language remain open. A response draft saved before this correction arrived was not delivered and has been removed from the transcript. No implementation change was made.

Discussion — Source-backed Activity board mock and visual rounds

User (verbatim):
good now i think instead of working with purely synthetic data in our mock we should produce our synthetic data from an actual view code the hacky way.

I suggest we use the activity board to do that.

I would also suggest we do some image rounds to how starting from the filter feature we move toward reaching the scope of the activity board view code.

Current work: Use the actual Activity board source and its owned query metadata as disposable mock material. Produce a first visual proposal showing filter context and surrounding view code. Boundaries, language and navigation remain open; image states are examples for review. Mock actions remain local and have no production effect.

Discussion — Direct rapid mock iterations replace generated images

User (verbatim):
ok image gen is dogshit it won't cut it and our ui editor is not yet ready.

i think what we need is to rapid fire the edit of the mock filter ui component to start with.

Current direction: Stop using generated design images and iterate directly on the runnable mock filter. First direct increment adds Reveal context to the existing filter row, reuses the shared source editor and view toolbar to inspect captured Activity board source, offers the captured syntax ancestry through a selector, and preserves the filter draft when returning. Source is read-only in this increment; source navigation does not execute code or change production behavior. The image proposal is rejected as the iteration medium, not accepted architecture.
